en: Hu Jizang composed:

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Er-yan Sheng-jue-da, practicing in accordance with the patience of conforming to the Dharma (anulomikī-dharmakṣānti), turning against the current of the five views, accumulating immeasurable merit, and abiding in the stage of Srotāpanna.
Below the section on Er-yan, it clarifies the fourth stage.

The text consists of four parts: first, the designation of the name; second, the establishment of the name of "patience" (kṣānti); third, the departure from hindrances; and fourth, the advancement in practice.
Regarding the first, the designation of the name, the text says: "The Bodhisattva named Īryāpatha-āryabuddhi-prativedha."
That which is called "flame" (jvālā) is here termed the "mother of wisdom" (prajñāmātṛ); since it advances toward the severance of discursive thought, it is called "awakened penetration.
Because the object can give rise to wisdom, the object is taken as the mother of wisdom.
Furthermore, another interpretation is that the *Bhūmi-sūtra* refers to the "Blazing Ground" (*Ārciṣmatī-bhūmi*), which is an explanatory metaphor.
The second stage establishes the name "Patience" (*kṣānti*); those who practice the patience that accords with the Dharma possess the lower grade of "Accordant Patience" (*anulomikī-kṣānti*).
The third section, "Freedom from Obstructions," consists of three sub-phrases:
first, reversing the flow of the five views; second, abiding in the first fruit; and third, freedom from the obstructions of the fetters.

Regarding the first, "reversing the flow of the five views," this clarifies that Bodhisattvas of the fourth stage are able to extinguish the habitual tendencies of the afflictions associated with the five views.
The *Bhūmi-sūtra* states: "With the view of self as the foremost, one completely distances oneself from them all.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "In the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), one abandons the innate view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and ignorance (*avidyā*)."
The Tripiṭaka Master said:
"In the Mahāyāna, there are specifically five views.
First is the view of arising and ceasing, which corresponds to the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) in the Hīnayāna."
Second, views regarding the four foundations of mindfulness impair right mindfulness;
right mindfulness serves as their antidote, analogous to the treatment for wrong views in the Hīnayāna.
Third, views concerning good and evil impair right effort; right effort is capable of performing all non-discriminative actions.
If a bodhisattva discriminates among wholesome dharmas, they will be unable to practice with diligence.

This corresponds to the "clinging to precepts and views" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and the four views regarding sentient beings in the Hīnayāna; these are the objects of the bodhisattva’s antidote. A bodhisattva does not perceive sentient beings as being distinct from the bodhisattva.
The five right views consist of right giving as the antidote for not seeing that dharmas exist.
When a bodhisattva practices the ninefold path and is able to counteract this flow of the five views, they first enter the stage of a bodhisattva srotāpanna.
Regarding the nine kinds of paths: first, practicing within birth and death is like taking bitter medicine for an illness;
second, associating with sentient beings is like being a great physician, who does not take account of the patient's vexations and disturbances;
third, exerting physical strength is like that of a servant who does not avoid cold or suffering, because his power is capable of endurance.

Fourth, entering into sensory desires like a merchant fearing the loss of his wealth; because for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, although one dwells in worldly pleasures, one does not excessively receive their karmic retribution.
Fifth, purifying the three karmas like a washerman who does not rest until they are clean;
sixth, not causing affliction to others.
Seventh, practicing the roots of goodness is like a person drilling for fire; once fire is obtained, one then remains still.
Eighth, cultivating meditative concentration is like having a servant.
Ninth, relying on wisdom is like a magician who does not conceive of the illusory assembly as real.
The source of this has not yet been seen; it will be detailed separately.
Regarding the second point, the stage of the *srotāpanna*, there are two interpretations:

first, within the context of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one suppresses afflictions by practicing the contaminated path (*sāsravamārga*) during the second and third stages, and permanently severs afflictions by practicing the uncontaminated path (*anāsravamārga*) during the fourth stage; upon first attaining the practice of the uncontaminated path, one is called a *srotāpanna*.

Regarding the second meaning: from the third stage (*bhūmi*) and below, one creates tainted karma (*sāsrava-karma*). On the first stage, one practices giving; on the second stage, one maintains precepts; on the third stage, one cultivates the eight dhyānas of tainted concentration. From the fourth stage upward, one cultivates the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), severs the three realms, and goes against the current of birth and death; this is called a *srotāpanna*.

Furthermore, this person severs the obstacles caused by the perception of self and others; being similar to the first fruit of the Lesser Vehicle (*śrāvaka*), they are given a name based on this resemblance.

Constantly possessing the divine eye, divine ear, knowledge of past lives, knowledge of others' minds, and the supernormal power of the body, they are able to extinguish all views within the three realms in every moment of thought. Moreover, for seven *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they have practiced the five supernormal powers, and the *pāramitās* as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have never been absent from their minds.

Regarding the five supernormal powers, such as the divine eye: Bodhisattvas on the third stage attain the five supernormal powers through the cultivation of the path while still in the state of outflows (sāsrava); those on the fourth stage attain the five supernormal powers while in the state without outflows (anāsrava) and partially realize the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya), though this is omitted here and not explicitly mentioned.
The manifestation of being free from the three fetters signifies the extinction of all views within the three realms.
Regarding the fourth stage of progress, the text states "by means of seven asaṃkhyeyas.
One should likewise formally designate its name and position, though the text omits them for brevity.

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Victorious Attainment, through the patience that accords with the Path, contemplates ten million truths (*nayuta-dharma*) by means of the four fearlessnesses. Because he has extinguished the doubts and afflictions of the three realms—such as the treatises of our own school, the treatises of external schools, medical prescriptions, crafts, and incantations—he declares, 'I am the Omniscient One. Since his marks of selfhood have been exhausted and he knows that each stage (*bhūmi*) has its point of emergence, it is called the 'Path of Emergence'."
"Victorious Attainment" (Jiṅdá) and below clarifies the fifth stage (*bhūmi*), consisting of five sections:

first, the designation of the name; second, the designation of patience (*kṣānti*); third, the threefold elucidation of the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*); fourth, the elucidation of the realization of the fruit; and fifth, the temporal duration of the practice.
First, regarding the designation of the name, the text states "the Bodhisattva who has attained excellence," which refers to the Ground of Difficult Victory (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*).
Second, regarding the explanation of "patience" (*kṣānti*), the text states "patience in accordance with the Path" (*anulomikī-kṣānti*).

In the fifth stage, the Bodhisattva cultivates the middle grade of compliant patience (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*), which accords with the contemplation of the path of suchness; this is called "patience that conforms to the path" (*anulomikī-mārga-kṣānti*).
Third, the explanation of the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) has two parts:
first, a general heading; second, a detailed exposition.
The initial general heading states that it is "by means of the four fearlessnesses.
The section beginning with "Observing the *nayuta*" provides the specific explanation of the fearlessness regarding omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
As for the term "*nayuta* *satya*," this is translated as "hundreds of millions of billions of truths."
The treatises of our own school are the Buddha’s twelve divisions of scripture;
the treatises of external schools are the four Vedas.
Medical prescriptions consist of the principles of the "sovereign and minister" and the "officials" as found in the *Bencao* (Pharmacopoeia).
"Artisan" refers to one who is skilled in the knowledge of constructing cities, moats, marketplaces, and the like.
"Incantation-master" refers to one who is proficient in esoteric arts and techniques.
"I am the Omniscient One" is the formulation of the fearlessness of omniscience.
The second [verse], "having extinguished that which is below the three realms," clarifies the fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

The afflictions such as doubt within the three realms are: first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); second, adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); and third, doubt (*vicikitsā*).
The afflictions of self and person have long been exhausted, and the two types of secondary afflictions have also been eliminated; now, for the first time, doubt is being removed.
Doubt is a functional affliction of the mind that takes the three realms as its basis and emerges from the three realms; therefore, it is called "doubt regarding the three realms," and so forth.
"One whose perception of a self has already been exhausted possesses no conceit of self.
"Knowing that each stage [of the path] has something from which one must emerge" clarifies the fearlessness of the path that exhausts suffering.
"That there is something from which one does not emerge is called an obstruction to the path."

Having reversed doubts regarding the three realms and cultivated immeasurable merit, one enters the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin; furthermore, by practicing for eight asaṃkhyeya kalpas and engaging in various dhāraṇī gates, one constantly practices the fearless contemplation without departing from the mind.
Regarding the four things from which he does not retreat, this clarifies his fearlessness in preaching that which obstructs the Path.
The Bodhisattva has four distinct forms of fearlessness, as named in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
first, retention through hearing; second, preaching the Dharma; third, answering difficult questions; and fourth, severing doubts.
Furthermore, this text explains the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) in relation to the Buddha’s four fearlessnesses; thus, it refers to the Buddha and Bodhisattvas.
Regarding the fourth fruit of realization, it states that by cultivating immeasurable merit, one enters the fruit of the *sakṛdāgāmin*.

In the Sanskrit original, it is called *sakṛdāgāmin*, which here is translated as "Once-returner" (*yīlái*). *Sakṛt* means "once," and *āgāmin* means "returner. This refers to one who has abandoned six grades of the defilements of the desire realm and the form realm through the path of cultivation.

Alternatively, the original text states: "In the fourth stage, one abandons the discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) of the desire realm; in the fifth stage, one abandons the discursive thoughts of the form realm; in the sixth stage, one abandons the discursive thoughts of the formless realm. Abiding in this state of attenuation, it is called 'the attenuation of afflictions' (*tanu-kleśa*)."
Another interpretation is as follows:

those who enter the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin* have completely severed the obstacles of the conceit of bodily purity (*kāya-śuci-māna*), yet a subtle obstacle of the habitual tendencies of affliction (*kleśa-vāsanā*) remains; thus, they resemble the *sakṛdāgāmin* of the Hīnayāna.
Alternatively, this person may be viewed in relation to the subsequent six stages as one who has only the status of a "once-returner" (*ekābhinivartana*).
The Tripiṭaka Master says:
"A Bodhisattva of the fifth stage still perceives the three realms within the remaining six stages; this is termed 'one who returns once'."
Regarding the fifth stage, it is called the "eight asaṃkhyeyas" because it follows upon the preceding seven numbers; thus, it is said to be eight.
*Dhāraṇī* is translated here as "that which can hold."

"Furthermore, constantly manifesting reality and abiding in the stage of compliant patience (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*), one practices the contemplation of the Middle Way; because one exhausts all afflictions—the causes and karmic accumulations that give rise to the three realms—and contemplates the single mark of neither existence nor non-existence as being non-dual, one realizes the stage of *anāgāmin*. Moreover, by practicing the illumination of the Middle Way for nine *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, the power of joy gives birth to [rebirth in] all Buddha-lands."
The sixth stage, the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), which constantly manifests below, consists of six sections:

first, the naming of the stage; second, dwelling in patience and cultivating contemplation; third, severing delusions; fourth, realizing the fruit; fifth, advancing in practice; and sixth, concluding with the Middle Way.
The first is called "Emergence," which constantly manifests reality.

The second is "Abiding in Patience and Cultivating Contemplation," which means abiding within the stage of *anulomikī-kṣānti* (conformable patience) to practice the contemplation of the Middle Way; it clarifies that Bodhisattvas of the sixth stage perform the contemplation of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).
The third is the extinction of delusion, which refers to the exhaustion of the causes of accumulation and the karma of accumulation within the three realms.
Although karma cannot be severed directly, by severing the afflictions, the causes of karma are extinguished of their own accord.
To speak of "neither existence nor non-existence" is precisely the manifestation of the Middle Way.

Regarding "one characteristic and no characteristic": one speaks of "one" in contrast to "two," and speaks of "no" in contrast to "existence"; therefore, it is called "one characteristic and no characteristic."
When the two are dispelled, the one is also eliminated; when existence is exhausted, non-existence also ceases. These are words of therapeutic remedy; do not form conceptual views regarding them.

The fourth is the realization of the fruit of *anāgāmin*; in the West this is called *anāgāmi*, which here is translated as "Non-returner. *Anā* means "not," and *gāmi* means "returning"; this refers to one who does not return to the desire realm.
This person, having received birth in the desire realm, will not return to the desire realm again.

Briefly stated, they sever the five lower fetters; in detail, they sever ninety-two: namely, the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the truths and the four proclivities abandoned through cultivation.
The Master of the Tripiṭaka said:
"Bodhisattvas of the sixth stage have four kinds of non-returning: first, non-returning to the mind of the two vehicles;
second, non-returning to demonic activities—demonic activities being the six sense objects;"
Third, the non-returner who delights in the Dharma;
fourth, the non-returner who relishes dhyāna.
During the fifth stage of progress, there are nine asaṃkhyeya kalpas.

The sixth is the contemplation of the Middle Way within the [sixth] fetter; it is called "practicing the illumination of the Middle Way," and by the power of one's vows, one attains birth in all Buddha-lands.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Xuanda cultivated the patience that delights in the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) for ten *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; he extinguished the causes of the accumulation of karma and its fruits within the triple world, and while dwelling in his final body, he fully accomplished immeasurable meritorious practices.
Xuan Da’s commentary below clarifies the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), which consists of seven sections:

first, the designation of the stage’s name; second, the progression of practice; third, the discernment of patience (*kṣānti*); fourth, the removal of hindrances; fifth, the accumulation of virtues; sixth, the summary of the stage’s status; and seventh, the transformative practices within the stage.
First, regarding the designation of the name: it is called "Bodhisattva Profoundly Attained," which refers to the Ground of Far-reaching (Dūramgamā-bhūmi).
Second, regarding the period of progress, the mention of "ten asaṃkhyeyas" refers to the quantity of time within that ground.

Third, regarding the discernment of patience (*kṣānti*): as for the phrase "joy in the non-arising of phenomena" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), it refers to attaining non-arising in the seventh stage; having begun to realize that the Dharma accords with the spirit, it is called the patience of the joy of the Dharma.
For example, the first stage (*bhūmi*) is called "Joyful" (*pramuditā*) because one attains the beginning of the ten stages;
this refers to the inferior grade of the contemplation of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Regarding the fourth [stage], "Freedom from Obstructions," which states that one "extinguishes the habitual causes, karma, and fruits of the three realms": this refers to the cessation of the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence), not its permanent exhaustion.
The first six stages are the causes for the cessation [of afflictions], while the seventh stage is the fruit of that cessation.
Alternatively, one may say that the sixth stage eliminates the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), while the seventh stage eliminates the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Furthermore, with respect to the causes and fruits of the karmic bonds associated with those [lower stages], these are not yet permanently exhausted at this [seventh] stage.

The fifth is the accumulation of merit. Regarding the phrase "dwelling in the final body": the exhaustion of the karmic retribution of the segmented existence (bhavāṅga) bound to the three realms is called "dwelling in the final body.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, based on causes and conditions from previous lives, a Bodhisattva at the seventh stage possesses a physical body.

Regarding the "seven stages" of the Śrāvaka stage: it is said that the physical body of the Śrāvaka attains enlightenment by relying on signs to understand the meaning; therefore, it is stated that there is a physical body at the seventh stage.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states, "The first stage is called the Dharma-body"; how much more so, then, would the seventh stage be a physical body?
The "fleshly body" (māṃsa-kāya) here refers to the fleshly aspect of the transformation body (nirmāṇa-kāya).
This is but one perspective; it should not be adhered to as a fixed tenet.

Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states, "At the very moment of first generating the mind [of enlightenment], one attains perfect awakening. How could one still possess a fleshly body at the seventh stage?

Regarding "all immeasurable merits are fully accomplished": this refers to the fact that while dwelling in his final body, his merits are collectively shown to be manifold; hence they are called "immeasurable.

His "knowledge of non-arising," "knowledge of exhaustion," and the "fivefold dharma-body" are all perfected. Dwelling in the tenth stage, the rank of the Arhat Brahmā Heaven, he constantly practices the contemplation of the three gates of emptiness, is fully endowed with hundreds of thousands of millions of samādhis, and extensively propagates the treasury of the Dharma.
Regarding "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpāda-jñāna*) and "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣaya-jñāna*): these specifically clarify the various merits of the final body.
For the time being, let us consider one way: when one looks forward solely to the exhaustion of the causes of the *pariccheda* (segmented) existence, it is termed "knowledge of exhaustion";
when the fruits of suffering no longer arise, it is termed "knowledge of non-arising."
The fivefold Dharma-body consists of untainted (anāsrava) morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Regarding the sixth stage of attainment, it is said that one dwells in the rank of an Arhat within the Brahma-heaven of the ten stages.
The Master of the Tripiṭaka said:
"There are three categories of Arhats: first, those at the ultimate limit of the triple world are called Arhats, as they see that the afflictions of the triple world are exhausted;
second, those whose fetters are exhausted are called Arhats, for on the seventh stage they see that the delusions of the triple world are neither existent nor non-existent."
The stage of Buddhahood at the end of the three realms of birth and death is called Arhat; therein one perceives that all afflictions are neither existent nor non-existent.
Furthermore, it is said that the exhaustion of birth and death within the limits of the segmented realm (pariccheda-jarā-maraṇa) is called Arhatship.
The station of Brahmā refers to the Brahmā King of the First Dhyāna.
Regarding the "ten stages," the three preceding stages of worthiness (śaikṣa) plus seven others are designated as the tenth stage.

Within the seventh stage, those who practice transformation are said to "practice the contemplation of the three emptinesses"—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—which constitute untainted wisdom (anāsrava-prajñā).
The "hundreds of thousands of myriads of samādhis" refers to untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*).
"Extensive transformation" means benefiting sentient beings.

Furthermore, regarding "one who has attained the patience of equal enlightenment" (*samyak-saṃbodhi-kṣānti-pratilabdha*): dwelling within the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they contemplate that the mind is quiescent, being a signless sign, a bodiless body, and a cognitionless cognition; yet they employ the mind to traverse the various directions, abiding in a state of detachment within the non-abiding abode.
Below "Equal Enlightenment" (*sambodhi*), the eighth stage is elucidated in five sections:

first, the designation of the stage’s name; second, the discrimination of patience (*kṣānti*); third, the illumination of signless contemplation (*animitta-darśana*); fourth, the conclusion regarding the rank of the great minister; and fifth, the period of advancing in practice.
The first indicates the name of the stage, referring to the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment, which is the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).
The second explains "patience," stating "one who dwells in the patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); this refers to the middle grade of the patience of non-arising.
Third, the clarification of contemplative understanding: "Contemplating the mind as the mind's own quiescent extinction" refers to the mind of non-attainment.

"The signless sign" means that while the signs of effortful activity characteristic of the seventh stage are absent, the signs of effortless spontaneity characteristic of the eighth stage are present.
"Bodyless body" means that while there is no body of effortful activity belonging to the seven stages, there is the effortless Dharma-body of the eighth stage.

"Knowledgeless knowledge" means that it is not like the knowledge of effortful activity in the seven stages, but rather the effortless knowledge from the eighth stage upward; this clarifies that at the eighth stage, one simultaneously illumines all phenomena, knowing them through non-knowing.

To "apply the mind to the directions of the manifold realms" means that the vehicle can transport all sentient beings; "directions" refers to the inclinations and tendencies of their dispositions, which are termed "directions.

Thus, the *Xici* says, "They gather according to their kind. Without fixed direction, one responds through transformation, appearing wherever beings may be; therefore, it is called "the direction of the manifold realms."

Although they universally transform all regions, they do not abide in birth and death; this is the effortless release of the untainted (*anāsrava*), and thus it is said that they dwell in detachment within non-abiding.

"While in existence, they constantly cultivate emptiness; while in emptiness, they constantly manifest the myriad transformations. They dualistically illumine all dharmas. Therefore, by knowing what is possible and what is impossible, and so forth, through the contemplation of the ten powers (*daśabala*) up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they are able to ascend to the stage of a Mahā-rāga, transforming sentient beings in all lands. For a thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they practice the dharma of the ten powers, with mind and mind in mutual correspondence, constantly entering the Samādhi of Seeing the Buddha.

Regarding those who constantly cultivate emptiness while remaining within existence: they clarify that though they are in existence, they are not defiled by it; thus, existence is unimpeded emptiness.
Knowing that existence is non-existence, they are able to render existence empty without impediment.
"Abiding in emptiness while constantly manifesting the myriad transformations" means that while quiescent, it is constantly active.
Since emptiness and existence are non-dual, it is said that it "shines upon all phenomena simultaneously.

Thus, one knows that "knowing what is a proper basis and what is not a proper basis" summarizes the clarification that both existence and non-existence are illuminated together: "emptiness" is termed the proper basis, and "existence" is termed the improper basis.
This may also be considered the first power, the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*).
Regarding the fourth stage of realization, the *mahārāja*: this is translated as "great minister.
Since he contemplates both emptiness and existence simultaneously and his transformative conduct rivals that of a Buddha, he is called a "great minister."
As the sutra says: "Śāriputra, the Buddha-dharma is the great general.
Fifth is the progression: practicing the dharma of the ten powers for a thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; the ten powers are explained separately.
"Mind and mind corresponding, constantly entering the samādhi of seeing the Buddha" means that because one attains the understanding of non-attainment, it is called "correspondence.
"Constantly entering the samādhi of seeing the Buddha" refers to the realization of the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* (the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha).

"Furthermore, regarding the spiritual transformation of the Radiance of Wisdom: abiding in the supreme and unsurpassed patience toward the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one extinguishes the characteristics of the mind and mental states. With the Dharma-eye, one perceives all phenomena; with the three eyes, one perceives form as empty. By the power of great vows, one is constantly born in all pure lands. Having accumulated the Samādhi of the Infinite Buddha-Radiance for ten thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one is able to manifest the spiritual powers of millions of billions of Ganges-sands of Buddhas. Abiding in the station of the Bhagavān, one also constantly enters the Buddha-Flower Samādhi."
The "Light of Wisdom" descends to clarify the Ninth Ground, which consists of seven sections:

first, the designation of the ground’s name; second, the explanation of patience (*kṣānti*); third, the cessation of evil; fourth, the illuminating function of the four eyes; fifth, birth through the power of vows; sixth, the period of progress; and seventh, the conclusion of the stage.
The first title is "Wisdom Light" (*Jñānaprabhā*), which refers to the Ground of Excellent Wisdom (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
Here, "wisdom" (*jñāna*) is *prajñā*, "light" (*prabhā*) is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and "spiritual transformations" (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa*) are liberation (*vimukti*).

The second explanation of patience (*kṣānti*) states: "Abiding in the supreme of the supreme patience of non-arising" means that within the patience of non-arising, this is the superior grade; compared to the middling grade of the preceding eight stages, it is superior to the inferior grade. Therefore, this ninth stage is said to abide in the supreme of the supreme patience of non-arising.

The third section, "Extinction of Delusion," explains that what is called the extinction of the mind and its mental characteristics refers precisely to the absence of ignorance regarding the limits of the mind.
The fourth section clarifies the differing modes of illumination and function of the four eyes.

Regarding "the Dharma-eye sees all dharmas": this clarifies that the illumination of the Dharma-eye regarding existence is the Knowledge of the Paths (mārgajñatā); because it is able to take existence as its object to deliver sentient beings, it is said that "the Dharma-eye sees all dharmas."
This is merely one way of explaining it and should not be adhered to as a fixed rule.
Regarding "the three eyes seeing form and emptiness": the three eyes are the flesh eye, the heavenly eye, and the wisdom eye.

The functions of these three eyes differ: the flesh eye and the heavenly eye see coarse and subtle forms respectively, while the wisdom eye sees emptiness. Because these three eyes function in combination, it is said that "the three eyes see form and emptiness."

The three eyes are distributed as follows: the eye of flesh (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) exists among the three stages of worthiness (*tri-piṭaka-śaikṣa*) prior to the stages; the dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*) is attained upon entering the stages (*bhūmi*);

and the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*) exists after the path (*mārga*). Generally speaking, each stage possesses all five eyes; however, here we clarify that within the context of the causal path (*hetu-mārga*), only four eyes are formally established.

The fifth is the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-bala*). Regarding the statement "may the power of aspiration always lead to birth in a pure land," this refers to benefiting sentient beings through an aspiration characterized by non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).
The sixth is the stage of progressive practice (*pratipatti-kāla*), which has two parts:
first, from "ten *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas" onwards, it clarifies the advancement in meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
Furthermore, he is able to manifest [his power] here below, clearly arising with supernatural powers (ṛddhi) to benefit sentient beings.

Seventh, regarding the establishment of the stages: "Abiding in the stage of Bhagavān" translates as "World-Honored One" (Shizun). It is also called "Breaking the Pure Ground" (Pojingdi); "Bhaga" means "breaking," and "Vān" means "pure ground."
As for what is called the Buddha-flower Samādhi, it is the Śūraṅgama-samādhi.

Furthermore, regarding the observation that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas abide in the patience of cessation (*śānti-kṣānti*): from the initial generation of the mind until now, having passed through a million *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas and cultivated merit for a million *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they ascend to the adamantine pedestal (*vajra-pīṭha*) of the liberation of all dharmas.
"Observing the Buddha" and below clarifies the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
The text consists of three sections:
first, it clarifies the functional capacities within the stages.

Good son, from the stage of "Patience through Practice" (*kṣānti*) down to "Consecration" (*abhiṣeka*), this second section, "Comparative Evaluation to Reveal Superiority and Manifest the Limits of Practice," distinguishes the cause from the fruit; it is also called the distinction between "seeing the nature" and "not seeing the nature."
From "Constantly practicing all [perfections]" below, the third section concludes by exhorting entry into the stages (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the first, the clarification of the functions within the stage: there are four functions.
First, "contemplating the Buddha" refers to the name of the stage of Dharma-cloud (*dharmameghā*).
"Second, abiding in the patience of quiescence" (nirvāṇa-kṣānti) is the designation of the name of this patience.
This tenth stage shares the same single patience as the Buddha and is combined as the thirteenth Dharma Master.
Regarding the statement "abiding in the patience of quiescence" (*śānti-kṣānti*): if considered specifically, it refers only to the inferior grade of the tenth stage, the patience of quiescence;
if considered generally, it clarifies that both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are termed as abiding in the patience of quiescence.

Regarding the duration of practice during the third stage, the *Prabhākārī-bhūmi*, the text states "passing through one million [kalpas]" and so forth, clarifying that the period of cultivation is extremely long; by analogy with what precedes it, this should be understood as spanning thirteen *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
Regarding "the merits of a million *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas," this clarifies that the practices initiated on the Ground of Radiance (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*) are vast and manifold.

Regarding "the fourth [ground] manifesting the limit of its stage as being supremely high," the text states: "ascending to the liberation of all dharmas and dwelling upon the Vajra Terrace. Here, the tenth ground is considered the Vajra Terrace.
Furthermore, this phrase may also indicate the cause by means of the result, designating the Buddha as the "Vajra Terrace.
Because the causes of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) have been fulfilled, the Buddha abides in the result of the Vajra Terrace.

“Good son! From the stage of *kṣānti* (patience) up to the *mūrdhan-samādhi* (summit samādhi), all are termed ‘subduing all afflictions,’ yet they lack the conviction that extinguishes all afflictions. They give rise to the wisdom of liberation that illumines the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), but this is not termed ‘seeing. What is called ‘seeing’ is *sarvajñā* (omniscience). Therefore, since ancient times I have always said that only a Buddha knows, sees, and awakens; from the *abhiṣeka-samādhi* (consecration samādhi) downward, including the stage of *kṣānti*, one does not know, see, or awaken.”
Only the Buddha possesses instantaneous understanding; this is not called "faith" for those who subdue [the afflictions] gradually.

Although wisdom arises and ceases, it is capable of being without arising and without cessation. If this mind were to cease, then there would be no defilements that would not cease. Being without arising and without cessation, one enters the principle and exhausts the Vajra-samādhi, becoming identical with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and equal to the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), yet one has not yet attained equality with the Peerless-Equally-Peerless.

"Good son, from 'the stage of practicing patience' (*śikṣā-kṣānti*) onwards, the second section—'Comparative Measurement Revealing Superiority and Clarifying the Limits of Practice'—consists of six sentences:

first, distinguishing the cause from the fruit; second, clarifying that the fruit differs from the cause; third, explaining why the cause differs from the fruit; fourth, explaining why the fruit differs from the cause; fifth, concluding the distinction between cause and fruit; and sixth, concluding the distinction between fruit and cause."

Regarding the first point, distinguishing the cause from the fruit: it is said that from the stage of "patience through practice" (*śikṣā-kṣānti*) up to the "consecration" (*abhiṣeka*), all are termed "subduing. From the stage of patience through practice until the "vajra-like samādhi," as long as even a single thought-moment of the fundamental category of afflictions has not yet been eliminated, a momentary delusion remains; thus, speaking generally, this is termed "subduing."
Furthermore, it is said that when the cause is contrasted with the fruit, the mind still carries afflictions and they are not yet eternally absent; therefore, it is called "subduing" (*vibhava*).

As the text says, "yet there is no belief that all is extinguished," this means that from the first stage through the third stage, within the position of *kṣānti* (receptive patience), one also illuminates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
It is not called "seeing" because the nature of seeing has not yet been clarified.
Furthermore, another interpretation states:
it is not called "seeing" because those in the causal stages of the ten bhūmis do not perceive the nature of the fruition; thus, it is termed "not seeing."
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Bodhisattvas of the ten stages see [the nature] but not clearly; at the stage of Buddhahood, it is seen from beginning to end.

Second, this demonstrates that the fruit differs from the cause: it says that what is called "seeing" is *sarvajñā* (all-knowing wisdom). Therefore, when I say that only a Buddha knows, sees, and awakens to it, this demonstrates that the vision of the Buddha-fruit perceives the nature with perfect clarity.

The third [section] explains that the cause differs from the fruit; the text states that "that which cannot be known, seen, or awakened to, from the consecration samādhi up to the stage of practicing patience," refers to the Vajra-samādhi of the tenth bhūmi.
The "patience of practice" refers to the thirty minds.
As for that which is not known, not seen, and not awakened to, it is because this is the stage of the cause (*hetu-avasthā*);

thus, one does not see the Buddha-nature. The fourth [section] explains how the fruit differs from the cause; the text states: "Only the Buddha has sudden understanding (*tun-jie*), which is not called 'faith' (*śraddhā*). Regarding "sudden understanding": when the myriad practices are fully perfected and the Buddha’s illumination of principle is exhaustive, it is therefore termed "sudden."

The fifth point concludes that the cause differs from the fruit; as for the phrase "gradually subduing," it means that although wisdom arises and ceases, this clarifies that the causal path is impermanent.
As for the phrase "being able to be without arising and without ceasing," it clarifies the ability to extinguish those afflictions of arising and ceasing.
Furthermore, another interpretation is as follows:
because one knows what is a cause and what is not a cause, and knows what arises and what does not arise, it is said that "one is able to be without arising and without cessation.

Within the sixth section, "The Result is Different from the Cause," there is first an explanation by way of the Dharma (the teaching), followed by an explanation by way of a simile, and finally the application [of the analogy].
The initial statement "this mind" refers to the mind of the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*).
If it is extinguished, it is the extinction of the ground of abiding ignorance; through the path of the cause of clarity, one becomes detached from arising and ceasing.
The statement that "there are no afflictions (*saṃkleśa*) that are not extinguished" clarifies the removal of obstacles external to affliction.
The statement that "there is neither arising nor ceasing" refers to ultimate purity.
Because it illuminates principle and exhausts its source, it is called the Samādhi of the Exhaustion of Principle (*li-jin sanmei*).
To say they are "identical to the limit of reality" means they equally converge upon non-attainment.
To be "equal to the dharma-nature" means to know that all dharmas are non-dual.
Yet, to be unable to be "equal to the unequaled" means one has not yet become identical with the Buddha.
"Just as if a person were to ascend a great high terrace and look down upon all things, perceiving them all without exception;
so too is it with one who dwells in the Samādhi of the Exhaustion of Principles."
"Constantly practicing all deeds, he fulfills the treasury of merit, enters the stage of the Bhagavat, and likewise abides eternally in the Buddha-wisdom samādhi.
The following is an analogy used for explanation.
It is said, "For example, suppose there is a person who ascends a great high platform"—this refers to the stage of the Tathāgata.
The Tripiṭaka Master says:
"The metaphors are fivefold."
First, it is supreme, for it is the pinnacle of all things.
Second, it is truly indestructible, like the fruit of Buddhahood, which is eternally abiding and difficult to ascend.
Third, it returns to the source, transcending both the ordinary and the sage.
Fourth, its self-nature is quiescent, for it is like the Buddha, being without arising or ceasing.
Fifth, it is the locus of peace and bliss, for it is like tranquil contemplation, wherein there is nothing that is not understood.
The statement, "Abiding in the samādhi of the exhaustion of principles is likewise," is the application of the analogy.
"Constantly practicing all lower-level deeds" concludes the third section on the stage of exhortation.

Entering the stage of the Bhagavat—here translated as the "Stage of Bestowing Virtue"—is so called because one can rain down the teaching of the Dharma; it is also named the "Stage of Breaking Through the Limits."
Because they are fully endowed with meditative concentration and wisdom, it is called the Buddha-wisdom samādhi. "Good son!

All such bodhisattvas are able to transform sentient beings within all the buddha-lands of the ten directions, correctly expounding the true meaning, receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, and penetrating the reality-mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), being no different from myself today."
"Good son," from this point downward, the direct answer consists of three sections: first, the brief answer; second, the detailed answer—these two parts are concluded;
now follows the third, the summary.
There are three parts:

first, it clarifies that the thirteen Dharma masters were able to propagate and transform others through the Mahāyāna; thus it says, "All these Bodhisattvas are able to transform and guide sentient beings throughout all the ten directions."
"Correctly expounding the correct meaning" (zhèngshuō zhèngyì) below marks the second section, which clarifies that the thirteen Dharma masters are able to expound the correct meaning.
"Correct meaning" refers to the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
"As I [have taught]" below marks the third section, which clarifies that what is taught is without difference.
This passage clarifies that these thirteen types of persons can transform beings equally to the Buddha; therefore, it says they are "equal and without difference.
The Buddha told King Prasenajit:

"After my parinirvāṇa, when the Dharma is about to perish, all kings and others should receive and uphold this Prajñāpāramitā and perform great Buddhist works. That all lands are established in peace and the myriad people enjoy happiness—all of this arises from this Prajñāpāramitā."
The Buddha addressed King Prasenajit; this concludes the second major section of the response, which exhorts [the king] to uphold [the teaching].
This section consists of seven parts:
first, a brief mention of the time and occasion, intended to clarify that the entrustment is made to the king and not to others.
"Great King, this is now the second descent, the place where the propagation and circulation of the sutra are proclaimed.
This is the third descent within that kingdom, which concerns the seven calamities.
Great King, this is the descent of the Prajñā; fourth is the praise of the merit of the Prajñā, which is able to extinguish the seven calamities."
"Great King, regarding 'I now cast down the five eyes' below: this fifth point raises the benefits of the meritorious virtues of the three periods of time.

Great King, regarding 'if in a future age' below: this sixth point clarifies that one who can practice according to the teachings shall be sent the protection of the five great Bodhisattvas, and is exhorted to create scriptures and images for offering."
"Great King, I now descend to the seventh and final exhortation to uphold this sutra.
Therefore, I entrust it to the various kings, and do not entrust it to bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās."
Why is this? Because he lacks royal power, he has not entrusted it to him.
You should receive, uphold, recite, and explain its meaning and principles.
Within the first entrustment, there are two parts:
first, clarifying the entrustment to kings to uphold the *prajñā*;

second, from "not entrusting to bhikṣus" onwards, clarifying that because they lack royal power and influence, they are not entrusted [with the responsibility], but are instead merely instructed to uphold, recite, and explain its meaning and principles.
Entrusting [the teaching] to a king has two meanings:
first, the ability to transform sentient beings who are difficult to transform;
second, the power to benefit great persons as the wind bends the grass. Since bhikṣus lack such powers, it is not appropriate to entrust [the teaching] to them.
“Great King!

That which I have now transformed consists of ten billion Sumeru mountains and ten billion suns and moons. Each Sumeru has four continents; within Jambudvīpa to the south, there are sixteen great kingdoms, five hundred middle kingdoms, and ten thousand small kingdoms.”
The second section clarifies the locations where the Prajñāpāramitā is extensively taught.
When it says, "Great King, the ten billion Mount Sumerus that I have now transformed," this collectively indicates the region of Jambudvīpa.

Below Jambudvīpa in the south, the various lands are specifically elucidated: first, the sixteen great nations; next, the five hundred intermediate nations; and finally, the ten thousand minor nations.

"In that land there are seven fearsome calamities; for the sake of these calamities, all kings shall lecture and recite the Prajñāpāramitā. Then the seven calamities will immediately cease and the seven blessings will arise, such that the myriad subjects will dwell in peace and happiness, and the sovereigns will rejoice."
"What are the difficulties?
This section, situated at the end of the [description of] that land, thirdly clarifies the seven difficulties.
The text consists of two parts:
First, it provides a general explanation that the power of the Dharma can eliminate the seven calamities and generate the seven blessings.
Next, from the passage beginning "What are the calamities? onwards, it specifically enumerates the seven calamities and clarifies how the power of this sutra can eliminate them.

Regarding the seven calamities: first, the sun and moon losing their proper courses; second, the aberrations of the lunar mansions; third, calamities of fire; fourth, calamities of water; fifth, calamities of wind; sixth, calamities of drought; and seventh, bandits.

"When the sun and moon lose their proper courses and the seasons run contrary to their order—whether a red sun appears, a black sun appears, or two, three, four, or five suns appear; or when the sun is eclipsed and lacks light, or when the solar disc appears with one, two, three, four, or five concentric halos—at such times of portentous transformation, to read and recite this sutra constitutes the first difficulty."
The first is the difficulty regarding the sun and moon.
Internally, there are fourteen points:
first, explaining "transgression of the proper measure," which is called transgressing the measure when one does not rely on the constant Way.
2. The reversal of the seasons; 3. the rising of red suns; 4. the rising of black suns;

5. the rising of two suns; 6. the rising of three suns; 7. the rising of four suns; 8. the rising of five suns; 9. solar eclipses; 10. a single halo; 11. a double halo; 12. a triple halo; 13. a quadruple halo; 14. a quintuple halo.
These fourteen kinds of phenomena are all the signs of calamities, famine, warfare, and pestilence.

When the twenty-eight lunar mansions lose their proper courses, and when Venus, comets, the wheel-star, the ghost-star, Mars, Mercury, the wind-star, the sword-star, the Southern and Northern Dous, the five great fixed stars, the stars of all national rulers, the stars of the Three Ducal Ministers, and the stars of the hundred officials—when all such stars manifest various portents, one should also read and recite this sutra; this constitutes the second difficulty.
The second is the difficulty regarding the constellations (*nakṣatra*).
As for the "twenty-eight," there are seven in each of the four directions; thus, four times seven makes twenty-eight.
Regarding "losing the proper measure" (*śīla-lopa*): it means that their movement does not conform to the regular path, hence it is called "losing the measure."
Venus is the planet Tàibáixīng (Venus).
The Tripitaka Master says:
In foreign lands, it is called the Star of the Celestial Teacher (Tiānshīxīng).
When one acts in accordance with the Dharma, the country prospers; when one deviates from the proper measure, there is scarcity.
As for the comet, it is called the Star of King Yama in foreign lands; wherever this star appears, there will inevitably be calamity and disaster.
Regarding the Wheel Star (Cakra): it possesses a radiance like a wheel. If the sun, moon, or the five planets pierce the center of the Wheel Star, the kingdom will be divided.
If the sun, moon, and five planets move to the right of the Wheel Star, the kingdom will be peaceful and happy; moving to the left is likewise unfavorable.

Regarding the Ghost Star (Gui Xing): if during the ninth lunar month the sun is situated in the northeast, and its movement is rapid, this indicates the passing of the seasonal period; if it approaches the zenith, ghosts and spirits will come to destroy the state and afflict the people with illness.
Mars is the planet of military operations and confusion; it presides over rebels. If it is high, rebels will rise up; if it is low, rebels will remain hidden.
If it is in the position of Zi (the northern direction), it is low; if it is in Wu (the southern direction), it is high.
Mercury is both the Moist Star and the Great White Star; if it is in the position of Yin, it is low, and if it is in the position of Shen, it is high.
It travels through one station for thirty days, completing one circuit in twelve months.

If one travels through the four regions of the cock, dog, pig, and rat, there will be no water; if one travels through the four regions of the hare, snake, sheep, and monkey, there will be much water; if one travels through the four regions of the ox, tiger, dragon, and horse, the water will be level—neither too much nor too little.

The wind-star is the planet Venus (*Śukra*). When it is in the position of the Tiger (*Vyāghra*), it is high; it moves through one position for thirty days, and when it moves through the position of the Monkey (*Vānara*), it is low.
If it is high, there is much wind and little rain; if it is low, there is much rain and little wind.
In the seventh month it is high, and in the first month it is low; from the eighth month to the first month it gradually descends, and from the second month to the seventh month it gradually ascends.
Regarding its movement in accordance with the sun, there are three types:

in the second, third, eighth, and ninth months it moves level with the sun; in the tenth, eleventh, twelfth, and first months—these four months—it moves ahead of the sun; and in the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh months—these four months—it moves behind the sun.
This is the practice that accords with the Dharma; to differ from this is to lose the measure and is not good.
As for the Star of the Knife (Kṛttikā), it is currently a full star, and its course through one region lasts two and a half years.

If it is at its highest point when in the position of the rabbit, or at its lowest point when in the position of the cock, then there will be much violence by the sword, and sentient beings will suffer from hunger and disease; if it is at its lowest point, there will be little violence by the sword.
The Southern Dipper and the Northern Dipper are not lunar mansions but luminaries.
The five great stars of the Five Towns are those of gold, wood, water, fire, and earth.

As for the stars of all national rulers, the Three Dukes, and the hundred officials—if auspicious stars enter the positions of these four stars, there will be great peace, stability, abundance, and joy; if malevolent stars enter them, there will be great suffering and affliction.
The various stars move together, deviating from their regular courses; hence it is said that they each manifest transformations.

If great kings or ministers govern the people unrighteously, indulging in license and self-indulgence, and the retribution of suffering is about to arise, then the sun and moon will wane or wax abnormally and the stars will lose their proper orbits. These serve as omens of inauspiciousness, thereby manifesting impending calamities.

If one can lecture upon and study the Mahāyāna and take refuge in the Triple Gem, calamities will depart according to their merit and the sun and stars will return to their proper courses; therefore, it is said that this sutra is also preached for such purposes.
"If a great fire burns the country, consuming all the people;

or if there are fires of ghosts, fires of dragons, fires of devas, fires of mountain deities, fires of humans, fires of trees and plants, or fires of bandits—should such strange calamities occur, one should likewise read and recite this sutra, as it serves as a protection against these three hardships."
The great fire burning the kingdom below constitutes the third fire-related calamity.
It has two parts;
first, the explanation of the seven kinds of fire.
The second section, "Furthermore, one should read this sutra," and below, clarifies that the power of the sutra can extinguish fire.
Regarding the seven kinds of fires: as for "ghost fire," it is when ghosts, out of anger toward sentient beings, produce evil fires at night; these also cause people to suffer from febrile illnesses.
As for "dragon-fire," it is the poisonous fire rained down by a wrathful dragon that causes people to suffer from boils and swellings; it is the supernatural fire obtained as a retribution.
As for "celestial fire," it is the fire of thunderbolts, so named after its celestial origin.
The "divine fire" refers to a supernatural manifestation.
There are two types of such spirits:
first, those arising from the anger of a rishi, whose fire is born of that wrath.
The two immortals recited incantations to cause demons and spirits to burn the houses of the common people.
As for "human fire," it is designated by its connection to humans;
the fire of trees and wood can be understood accordingly.
Regarding "bandit fire": when bandits throw fire [upon the land], it is called "bandit fire.
Furthermore, for those who read and recite this sutra, the power of the sutra can extinguish such fires.

When great waters flood and submerge the populace, when the seasons run contrary to their natural order—such as rain in winter and snow in summer; when there is thunder, lightning, and crashing peals in winter; when ice, frost, hail, and sleet fall in the sixth month; when red water, black water, or blue water rains down; when mountains of earth and mountains of stone rain down; when sand, gravel, and stones rain down; when rivers flow upstream; and when mountains float and stones drift—when such calamities occur, one should also read and recite this sutra. These constitute the four hardships.
Below "great water" is the fourth water-related calamity.
This refers to when water is needed but unavailable, or when it is abundant where it is not required.
Frost, hail, and the like all belong to the category of water-related calamities.

If red water rains down, there will be much warfare; if black water rains down, it will cause disease; if green water rains down, there will be much famine; if earth, stones, and sand rain down, the *ṛṣis* and *rākṣasas* are angry.
If rivers flow upstream and the ocean overflows, there will be bandits.

"When great winds blow and kill the myriad people, and the lands, mountains, rivers, and trees all perish at once; when untimely winds—black winds, red winds, blue winds, celestial winds, earthly winds, fire-winds, and water-winds—occur during such transformations, one should also read and recite this sutra; this constitutes the fifth hardship."
The fifth is the danger of wind.
This also has two parts:
first, the enumeration of the seven winds; [second, their detailed explanation].
The second part, "Furthermore, by reading this sutra," indicates that the power of the sutra can transform and extinguish [the calamities].
"Black wind" refers to the winds on the seashore that blow black sand;
"red wind" refers to the red sand.
The "blue wind" refers to the blue sand.
The "heavenly wind" and "earthly wind" refer to the yang of heaven and the yin of earth.
The "fire wind" refers to hot wind.

"When heaven, earth, and the lands suffer from excessive drought, and blazing fires rage everywhere; when the hundred grasses wither from parching heat and the five grains fail to ripen; when the soil is scorched and the myriad people perish—when such calamities occur, one should still read and recite this sutra; this constitutes the sixth hardship."
"When the heavens and earth suffer from excessive heat below, this is the sixth difficulty of drought; its textual characteristics can be known.

When bandits come from the four quarters to invade, and rebels arise within the country and abroad—whether as fire-bandits, water-bandits, wind-bandits, or ghost-bandits—and the common people fall into chaos and turmoil as the calamity of war breaks out—one should likewise read and recite this sutra during such times of anomaly; these constitute the seventh difficulty."
"Below, regarding the uprising of bandits from the four quarters, this is the seventh calamity of bandits.

'Great King! This Prajñāpāramitā is the divine root of the consciousness of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and all sentient beings; it is the parent of all kings. It is also called the Divine Talisman, the Ghost-Averting Pearl, the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel, the State-Protecting Jewel, the Mirror of Heaven and Earth, and the Dragon-Treasure King. "
In the "Great King's Prajñā" section, the fourth part praises the virtue of prajñā for its ability to extinguish the seven calamities.
The text consists of two parts:
first, praising prajñā as inconceivable; [the second follows].
Next, from "The Buddha then said to the Great King" onwards, the second section clarifies that since Prajñāpāramitā extinguishes the seven calamities, it exhorts people to make offerings to it.
Within the initial praise of Prajñāpāramitā, there are eight phrases.

First, regarding the clarification that Prajñāpāramitā can serve as the fundamental essence of the mental consciousness and spirit of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas: Prajñāpāramitā is non-attainment (*anupalambha*). Because all Buddhas awaken to non-attainment by means of Prajñāpāramitā, Prajñāpāramitā is the Mother of the Buddhas; therefore, it is said to be the "basis of the Buddhas."

The fundamental nature of the mind-consciousness of all sentient beings is originally unattainable; it is only through the conditions of deluded conceptualization that the distinctions of the six realms of existence arise. If one can realize that these delusions ultimately have no existence and thus return to *prajñā*, it is therefore said to be the fundamental nature of the mind-consciousness of all sentient beings.
The mind (citta), consciousness (vijñāna), and spirit (manas) are one in essence, differing only in name. Furthermore,
another interpretation holds that the mind, consciousness, and spirit are fundamentally the *tathāgatagarbha*, which is the root of birth and death.
Regarding the statement that Prajñāpāramitā is the parent of all kings: because Prajñā can protect the realm, it is likened to parents.

It is also called a "divine talisman" (śenfu) because it can penetrate the realm of reality as it is (yathābhūta), subdue the celestial Māras and non-Buddhists (tīrthika), and protect all mundane and supramundane roots of goodness; therefore, it is likened to a divine talisman.
The "Demon-Averting Jewel" is so called because it can eliminate the perils posed by ghosts and spirits.
The "Wish-Fulfilling Jewel" is so called because Prajñā is obtained according to one's wishes.
The "Nation-Protecting Jewel" is so called because the power of Prajñā can cause the land to be peaceful and secure.
The "Mirror of Heaven and Earth" refers to the fact that *prajñā* illuminates the world as being devoid of intrinsic existence.
The "Divine King of Dragon Jewels" refers to the fact that *prajñā* can bring forth all benevolent deities; thus, he is called the Divine King of Dragon Jewels.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"You should prepare banners of nine colors, nine zhang in length;
and flowers of nine colors, two zhang in height."
"A thousand-branched lamp, five *zhang* in height;
nine jade boxes and nine jade cloths, and likewise seven-jeweled tables, upon which the sutra scrolls are placed.
From "The Buddha said to the Great King" onwards, the second section clarifies the exhortation for people to make offerings, which contains two parts:
First, there is the individual offering;
following this, one makes a general offering of flowers and incense each day.
Within the initial individual offerings, first the six types of offering articles are enumerated, and second, the Prajñāpāramitā is brought forth and offered.
The first six items are: first, a banner; second, flowers; third, lamps; fourth, a jade casket; fifth, a jade cloth; and sixth and seventh, a table of the seven treasures.

"Whenever the King travels, these are always placed before him at a distance of one hundred paces. This dharma-relic constantly emits a thousand rays of light, causing the seven calamities not to arise and transgressions not to occur within a thousand li."

When the king resides there, he shall construct a pavilion of the seven treasures, within which is a high seat made of the seven treasures. Upon this he shall place the sutra scrolls and offer daily worship, scattering flowers and burning incense, as if serving his own parents or serving Śakra, Lord of Devas.
Regarding the second method of making offerings, there are five internal points:
first, take out the Prajñā and place it upon the table;
second, when the King travels, have the Prajñā precede him.
First, while the three kings traveled but a hundred paces, Prajñā emitted light for a thousand *li*;
second, she caused that within a thousand *li* there were no seven calamities, which was her benefit;
third, when she stayed there, she created a throne of the seven treasures and placed Prajñā upon it.
The second day, the text below provides a general explanation of making offerings, which can be understood through both the literal teaching and its metaphorical meaning:
"Great King!

I now see clearly with my five eyes that all kings of the three periods of time have become sovereign emperors and rulers by virtue of having served five hundred Buddhas in past lives; this serves as great benefit for all sages and arhats who come to be born within those kingdoms."
"When a king's merit is exhausted, all holy beings will abandon him.
When all holy beings have departed, the seven calamities will inevitably arise.
"Great King, I have now finished the fifth eye, which clarifies the benefits of the three periods of time, causing people to believe and uphold it."
The text consists of three parts.

The first clarifies that [the King] has illuminated all [realms] with the five eyes and served five hundred Buddhas and others, demonstrating his long-term offerings to many sages while currently occupying the royal throne.
This indicates that a sage has descended; secondly, it clarifies that a sage has been born in this country to bring about great benefit.
If a king were to descend, his threefold merit would be exhausted and he would find it difficult to be reborn.
“Great King!

If in future ages there are kings who uphold the Triple Gem, I shall dispatch five Great Power Bodhisattvas to protect their kingdoms: first, the Bodhisattva Vajraghoṣa, who will go to protect that kingdom holding a thousand-jeweled wheel;
second, the Bodhisattva Nāgarājaghoṣa, who will go to protect that kingdom holding a golden-wheel lamp;”
The Bodhisattva Fearless Roar of the Ten Powers held a vajra in his hand and went to protect that land;
the Bodhisattva Roar of Thunder and Lightning held a net of a thousand jewels in his hand and went to protect that land;
the Bodhisattva Roar of Immeasurable Power held five thousand sword-wheels in his hand and went to protect that land.
"These five great bodhisattvas and five thousand great ghost-king deities have brought great benefit to your kingdom; you should establish their images and make offerings to them.

O Great King, if in future ages there are those who follow this teaching according to the sixth illumination, you should dispatch these five great bodhisattvas as protectors and exhort the creation of images for worship.
The text consists of four parts:
first, a general explanation that five great bodhisattvas will constantly protect the kingdom in future ages;
second, a specific listing of the names of these five great bodhisattvas.
"Third, three to five thousand great deity-kings will bring great benefit to your kingdom;
fourth, they will cause images to be established for worship.
Great King!"

I now entrust the Three Jewels to all you kings: those of the kingdoms of Vaiśālī, Kośala, Śrāvastī, Magadha, Vārāṇasī, Kāśī, Kuśinagara, Kauśāmbī, Kuru, Kaśmīra, Mithilā, Karakaṇḍa, Gandhāra, Sādhā, Saṃghāṭa, Kanyakubja, and Pāṭaliputra. All such kings as these should receive, uphold, and practice the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Great King, I now descend for the seventh time to exhort you to receive and uphold this sutra.
This section has three parts;
the first clarifies the entrustment to all kings."
The second section lists sixteen countries;
as in all such cases below, the third section encourages the upholding [of the teaching].
This sutra clarifies only seventeen countries, so why does it say sixteen?
Answer:
In the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*, there are sixteen great kingdoms.

At that time, the great assembly of Asura kings, having heard from the Buddha the seven fearsome calamities of the future age, their body hair stood on end and they cried out with loud voices, saying:
"I vow not to be born in that land.

At that time, the sixteen great kings entrusted the affairs of state to their younger brothers, left the household life to practice the Way, and contemplated the four great elements and the four colors as signs of transcendence; they practiced the contemplation of the four great elements and the four colors as being without self and empty of consciousness.
At that time, from among the great assembly, including the Asura Kings and those below them, the third major section of the response explains how the assembly benefited upon hearing the Dharma.
This section consists of six parts;
first, a general explanation of how the great assembly, upon hearing the teaching, gave rise to vows.
The twenty-sixth king realized the Way;
the thirty-eighth Brahmā and others attained benefit;
and the fourth, nine hundred billion bodhisattvas, realized the fruits of the path.
Fifty thousand bodhisattvas resolved to attain benefit in future lives;
six hundred million bodhisattvas attained manifest perfect enlightenment.
During the first period, the assembly, hearing the discourse on the seven fearsome calamities, had their body hairs stand on end and made vows not to be born in those lands.
The twenty-sixth section, "The Kings Attaining Benefit," has two parts:
first, it clarifies how the sixteen kings entrusted their kingdoms to their younger brothers and made vows to leave the household life;
second, it clarifies their cultivation of the path.
Within this, there are again two parts:
first, the two sections on the path of cultivation through the contemplation of provisional characteristics;
second, from the thirty kinds of patience (*kṣānti*) downward, the explanation of entering the path through actual practice.

Regarding the initial contemplation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the four secondary forms (*upādāyarūpa*) as the "superior manifestations," these constitute the eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Contemplating the four great elements internally constitutes the first four spheres of mastery. Contemplating the four great elements internally while contemplating a small amount of external form without breaking down the internal and external forms constitutes the first sphere of mastery. Contemplating the four great elements internally while contemplating a large amount of external form constitutes the second sphere of mastery. Having no conception of the four great elements internally while contemplating a small amount of external form constitutes the third sphere of mastery. Having no conception of the four great elements internally while contemplating a large amount of external form constitutes the fourth sphere of mastery.
This is the contemplation that destroys internal forms while not destroying external forms.
As for the latter four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), blue, yellow, red, and white are combined to form eight spheres of mastery.
Because the contemplation of the eight spheres of mastery is accomplished, they are called "the signs of transcending" (*abhibhava-nimitta*).
Next, the contemplation of the ten universal bases (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*) is explained.

The four great elements and the four derivative forms constitute eight; adding the base of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), which is the state of having no location, the base of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*), and the base of infinite space (*ākāśāyatana*), these three together form the ten universal bases.
Because the contemplation of the ten *kṛtsnāyatanas* (totalities) is perfected, it is called "entering the aspect of practice.

The thirty *kṣāntis* (patiences) are the marks of the first stage (*bhūmi*), while the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is the mark of the ninth stage. Therefore, Great King, you shall abandon the body of an ordinary person and enter the body of the sixth dwelling; you shall abandon the sevenfold retributive body and enter the eighth dharma-body, thereby realizing the *prajñāpāramitā* of all practices.
Below the thirty patiences (*kṣānti*), next is explained the entry into the Path through actual practice (*satyābhisamaya*).

The two types of contemplation on provisional characteristics (*prajñapti-lakṣaṇa*) belong to the stages prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*), while the thirty patiences belong to the grounds themselves.
Each of the ten grounds has three moments of mind, totaling thirty patiences.
Regarding the "characteristics of the first stage," this refers to the very first stage.
Regarding the "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-satya*), this clarifies that the attainment of the ultimate truth is accomplished in the first stage, serving as the preparatory phase for the ninth stage.
Regarding the "nine stages," these refer to the remaining nine stages beginning with the Stage of Freedom from Defilement (vimalā-bhūmi).

"Abandoning the body of an ordinary person and entering the body of the sixth stage" means abandoning the body of an external ordinary person and entering the body of the six stages beginning with the lineage (gotra-bhūmi).

Regarding "abandoning the seven retribution bodies to enter the eighth dharma-body": this means abandoning the seven preparatory stages (*prayoga*) prior to the [first] ground and attaining the eighth dharma-body of the first ground.
Alternatively, it may also mean abandoning the body of effortful application (*sābhoga*) of the preceding seven grounds and entering the effortless dharma-body from the eighth ground upward.

The eighteen Brahmā heavens and the Asura kings attained the contemplation of the Three Vehicles and entered the same realm of non-arising. They further scattered flowers as an offering: flowers of emptiness, flowers of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), flowers of the sages, flowers of compliance, flowers of non-arising, flowers of the joy of the Dharma, vajra flowers, flowers of the Middle Way through the contemplation of conditions, and flowers of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. These they scattered upon the Buddha, as well as upon the assembly of nine hundred billion great bodhisattvas and all other members of the assembly who had realized the fruits of the stages of the Path. They scattered flowers of the emptiness of mind, flowers of the tree of mind, flowers of the six *pāramitās*, and flowers of wondrous awakening upon the Buddha and the entire great assembly.
Below the section on the eighteen Brahmā heavens and the Asura kings, the third part clarifies how the various devas obtain benefits.
This section is divided into two parts:
first, the accomplishment of the contemplations of the three vehicles and the attainment of the benefit of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Second is the offering of scattered flowers.
Within this scattering of flowers, there are two parts:
first, scattering the flowers of the five patiences; second, scattering the flowers of the two vehicles.
The flowers of the five patiences are the flower of emptiness, the flower of the dharma-nature, and the flower of the patience of submissiveness prior to the stages.
The flowers of the sages are the flowers of the patience of faith on the first, second, and third stages.
The "Flower of Accordant Patience" refers to the flowers of accordant patience in the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages.
The "Flower of Non-arising" refers to the flowers of the patience of non-arising in the seventh, eighth, and ninth stages.
The "Vajra Flower" refers to the flower of the tenth stage.
The "Buddha-flower" refers to the flower of the patience of cessation (*śānti-kṣānti*).
Next, the flowers of the two vehicles are distinguished.
Regarding the "flower of the middle way through conditional observation," this refers to the flower of the Middle Vehicle of the *pratyekabuddha*.
The flowers of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the flowers of the śrāvakas.
Their scattering upon the Buddha is an act of making offerings.
As for the nine hundred billion great bodhisattvas and their assembly mentioned below, this constitutes the fourth section: the attainment of benefits.
The text has two parts:
first, it clarifies how the great assembly of nine hundred billion bodhisattvas attained awakening and received benefits;
second, it clarifies how they attained benefits through the offering of scattered flowers.

The text states that "realizing the traces and fruits of the Way" means that because one attains the understanding of the first stage (*bhūmi*), it is called "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*). Thus, that which enables passage is termed the "Way" (*mārga*), and because that Way enables progress, it is called a "trace" (*padasthāna*). Because awakening and understanding are fulfilled, it is called a "fruit" (*phala*).

Next, for the inner offering, there are four kinds of causal and resultant flower offerings: the "flower of the emptiness of mind" is the flower of the principle of emptiness and non-arising; the "flower of the tree of mind" is the flower of the tree of intention; the "flowers of the six pāramitās" are the flowers of practice; and the "flower of wondrous enlightenment" is the flower of the Buddha-stage.
Scattering [flowers] over the Buddha is an act of offering.

Ten thousand bodhisattvas, mindful of sentient beings in future ages, immediately realized the Samādhi of Wondrous Enlightenment, the Samādhi of Perfect Clarity, the Vajra Samādhi, the Samādhi of Worldly Truth, the Samādhi of Ultimate Truth, and the Samādhi of the Supreme Truth; these three samādhis of truth are the King of All Samādhis.

Below [the section on] the ten thousand bodhisattvas, the fifth clarifies how the ten thousand bodhisattvas contemplate sentient beings of future ages so that they may attain awakening and realize samādhi.
That which is called the "Samādhi of Sublime Awakening" is also named the "Samādhi of the Exhaustion of Principle."
The Samādhi of Perfect Clarity (*yuanming sanmei*) is so called because it illuminates principle exhaustively.
The Vajra Samādhi is so called because it is firm and indestructible.

The Samādhi of Worldly Truth (*shidi sanmei*) is so called because it clarifies the characteristics of meditative concentration according to what is perceived by ordinary beings; hence, it is termed "worldly truth."
The samādhi of the Truth of Reality (satyadharma-samādhi) refers to the partial truth as perceived by those of the Two Vehicles; therefore, it is called the "Truth of Reality.
The samādhi of the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya-samādhi) is precisely the Middle Way of the Ultimate Truth.
Within the Dharma, this is the most refined and undispersed; therefore, it is called "the foremost" and is also named the Samādhi of True Reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
This samādhi is the sovereign of all samādhis, for it universally encompasses all dharmas. Just as a king is able to exercise supreme command, it is thus named the "Sovereign of All."
He also attained countless other samādhis, such as the Samādhi of the Seven Treasures, the Samādhi of the Twenty-five Existences, and the Samādhi of All Practices.
Furthermore, ten billion bodhisattvas ascended to the Vajra-Pinnacle and manifested the attainment of perfect enlightenment.
The samādhi of the seven riches consists of: first, faith; second, precept-keeping; third, shame; fourth, remorse; fifth, extensive learning; sixth, wisdom; and seventh, relinquishment.
There are twenty-five samādhis that destroy the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*).
By attaining the stainless samādhi (*vimala-samādhi*), one can destroy the state of existence in hell.
By attaining the non-retrogressive samādhi (*avaivartika-samādhi*), one can destroy the state of existence as an animal.
By attaining the Samādhi of Mental Joy, one can destroy existence as a hungry ghost;
by attaining the Samādhi of Rapture, one can shatter existence as an asura;
by attaining the Samādhi of Sunlight, one severs existence in Pūrvavideha.
Attaining the Moonlight Samādhi, he severed existence in Aparagoyānī;
attaining the Blazing Heat Samādhi, he severed existence in Uttarakuru;
attaining the Illusion-like Samādhi, he severed existence in Jambudvīpa.
He attains the samādhi of immovability regarding all dharmas and severs existence in the realm of the Four Heavenly Kings.
He attains the samādhi of being difficult to subdue and severs existence in the realm of the Thirty-three Gods.
Attaining the Samādhi of Pleasing Intent, one cuts off existence in the Yāma Heaven.
Attaining the Samādhi of Blue Color, one cuts off existence in the Tuṣita Heaven.
Attaining the Samādhi of Yellow Color, one cuts off existence in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven.
