Attaining the red-colored samādhi, one cuts off existence in the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).
Attaining the white-colored samādhi, one cuts off existence in the First Dhyāna.
Attaining the various-colored samādhis, one cuts off existence in the Great Brahmā Heaven (Mahābrahmā).
Attaining the Twin Samādhi, one severs existence in the second dhyāna.
Attaining the Thunder-Sound Samādhi, one severs existence in the third dhyāna.
Attaining the Abiding-Rain Samādhi, one severs existence in the fourth dhyāna.
Attaining the Samādhi Like Space, one severs existence in the Heaven of No-Thought (Āsaṃjñika).
Attaining the Samādhi of Illuminating Objects, one severs existence as a Pure Abode Anāgāmin.
Attaining the Samādhi of Non-obstruction, one severs existence in the Sphere of Infinite Space (Ākāśānantyāyatana).
Attaining the Samādhi of Permanence, one severs existence in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness.
Attaining the Samādhi of Bliss, one severs existence in the Sphere of Nothingness.
Attaining the Samādhi of Self, one severs existence in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
This is called the Bodhisattva attaining the samādhi that destroys the twenty-five states of existence (pañcaviṃśati-bhava). These are:

the four modes of birth, the four evil destinies, the Brahma kings, the six heavens of the desire realm, the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, the state of non-conception, and the five Pure Abodes.
Furthermore, there were ten billion bodhisattvas who descended; the sixth of these ten billion bodhisattvas attained Buddhahood.
Chapter Eight: Entrustment (*Parindanā-parivarta*). The *Renwang Huguo Banruo Boluomi Jing* consists of three sections; this is now the third, the section on the Propagation of the Teaching.

Regarding the term "entrustment" (parindanā): it clarifies that the Tathāgata earnestly entrusts [this teaching] to kings and exhorts the multitude of bodhisattvas; hence it is called the "Chapter on Entrustment.
This chapter is divided into four sections:
the first is the admonition and command to Candraprabha to universally encourage its circulation, thereby clarifying the entrustment.
Following the section on the five corruptions of the later age, the second part consists of seven sections that separately admonish all kings and the fourfold assembly of disciples.

Under the heading "At that time, the sixteen great kings heard the Buddha’s seven admonitions," the third part clarifies how the kings did not exercise control over the fourfold assembly of disciples.
Under the heading "At that time, the immeasurable great multitude," the fourth part clarifies how the assembly joyfully accepted and upheld [the teachings].
Within the preceding general exhortation for circulation, there are again three parts:
first, the admonition to Candraprabha, clarifying the timing of the Dharma’s extinction;
second, from "The Three Jewels of this sutra" onwards, clarifying the person to whom it is entrusted.
Third, following the section "for the sake of the sentient beings of the three realms," this clarifies the benefits of its circulation.
The Buddha told King Prasenajit: "I exhort you all:

eighty years, eight hundred years, or eight thousand years after my parinirvāṇa, when there shall be no Buddha, no Dharma, and no Saṃgha, and no faithful men or women, at that time this Sūtra and the Three Jewels shall be entrusted to various kings and the fourfold assembly of disciples. You must receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain its meaning, opening the path of the wisdom of emptiness for the sentient beings of the three realms, practicing the seven preliminary noble practices, and transforming all sentient beings through the ten virtuous actions."
Regarding the statement "eighty years," this refers to the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

During the first hundred years following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, five patriarchs each upheld the Dharma for twenty years. Kāśyapa, Ānanda, and Madhyāntika—these three had personally witnessed the Buddha’s transformations; they practiced the Dharma as if the Buddha were still in the world, and thus the Dharma did not perish.
These three [masters] passed sixty years.
The fourth, Śāṇakavāsin, and the fifth, Upagupta—these two masters each upheld the Dharma for twenty years.
Śāṇakavāsin shall live for eight hundred years; because he will not personally witness the Buddha’s transformative power, the Dharma of majestic deportment will perish.
When it is said that eight hundred years [will pass], this refers specifically to the extinction of the True Dharma (saddharma).
Within the first five hundred years, twenty-five masters transmitted the teachings in succession, all of whom were sages; therefore, the realization of the Dharma did not perish.
Within the sixth and seventh centuries, two individuals—Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna—transmitted the Dharma; because these propagators of the Dharma were powerful, the Dharma did not perish.
During the eight hundred years thereafter, other people will propagate the Dharma; however, because these individuals are weak, they will cause the Dharma to perish.
As for the mention of "eight thousand years," this refers to the extinction of the Semblance Dharma at the end of the age.

Because sentient beings in the age of the final dharma delight in practicing false teachings and despise the true dharma, the true dharma does not prevail; thus, it is said that the two periods of the Semblance Dharma and the Final Dharma will perish.

However, according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, during the Semblance and Final Ages there will be one hundred and twenty thousand great bodhisattvas who skillfully uphold my teaching; therefore, my teaching shall not perish.
Since this refers to those who were previously ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), it is said that [the Dharma] has been extinguished.
The statement that there are no Buddha, Dharma, or Saṅgha precisely clarifies the extinction of the Dharma; therefore, it was necessary to entrust [the teachings].
The mention of the absence of faithful men and women clarifies that, as there were previously no Three Jewels to take refuge in, there was no basis for generating faith.
Because they slandered and reviled the Triple Gem due to a lack of faith, [the Dharma] was not manifested for them.
Second, regarding the clarification of those to whom it is entrusted, there are two parts:
first, the entrustment to the king; because he possesses great power and his merit in protecting the Dharma is strong, he is entrusted with it first.
The second section, the entrustment to the four classes of disciples, is a universal entrustment to all sentient beings, because these four classes encompass all sentient beings without exception.

The third section clarifies the benefits of its circulation; the internal text states that it "opens the path of empty wisdom for sentient beings of the three realms," meaning that by realizing the liberation of non-attainment, one opens the path of empty wisdom. Thus, it is called "opening the path of empty wisdom."
It further states: "Because one realizes the principle of the two kinds of selflessness, it is said that the path of wisdom regarding emptiness is opened.

As for the statement "practicing the seven stages of the worthy," these are the seven preparatory means (*saptopāya*): first, the contemplation of the five stabilizing minds; second, the stage of distinct mental applications; third, the stage of general mental applications; fourth, the stage of heat (*uṣmagata*); fifth, the stage of summits (*mūrdhan*); sixth, the stage of patience (*kṣānti*); and seventh, the stage of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).

Regarding the statement that the ten wholesome actions transform all sentient beings: first, not killing; second, not stealing; third, not engaging in sexual misconduct; fourth, not speaking falsely; fifth, not using harsh speech; sixth, not engaging in divisive speech; seventh, not engaging in frivolous speech; eighth, not coveting; ninth, not being angry; and tenth, not holding wrong views.
By means of these ten practices, one teaches and transforms sentient beings; therefore, it is said that "the ten wholesome practices transform all sentient beings.
This concludes the general exhortation for the circulation [of this teaching].

"In the future age of the five turbidities, the fourfold assembly of disciples—bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs—as well as the eight classes of gods and dragons, all spirit-kings, kings and ministers, and crown princes and sons of kings, will rely on their own high status and nobility to destroy my Dharma. They will openly establish restrictive laws, forbidding my fourfold assembly of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs from leaving home to practice the Way. Furthermore, they will prohibit the making of images of the Buddha or stupas of the Buddha. They will establish offices of supervision to control the masses and maintain registers of the monks; they will have bhikṣus stand on the ground while laypeople sit upon high seats. Soldiers and slaves will become bhikṣus, receiving special invitations for alms according to their own rules. Bhikṣus who are personal acquaintances will act with a single mind, while bhikṣus who are close friends will hold communal assemblies to seek merit. These will be like the practices of non-Buddhists; none of them are my Dharma."
"You should know that at that time, the True Dharma will soon be extinguished.
Following the section on the five corruptions, there is a second part consisting of seven distinct gates of specific admonitions, which comprise seven separate points:
first, one must not obstruct others from leaving the household life, and so forth.
Second, one must not allow secular officials to govern the Sangha;
third, one must not bind or restrain bhikṣus;
fourth, one must not preach the sūtras in an unrighteous manner, like a worm within the body of a lion.
Fifth, one must not employ bhikṣus like soldiers or slaves;
sixth, one must clearly understand that committing unrighteous acts incurs transgression and should be restrained so as not to be done, for such actions create faults and destroy the land;
seventh, one must not rely upon the Buddha-dharma to seek worldly fame or profit.
If one commits these seven acts, one violates the teachings and loses the principle, such that the practice of the Way cannot be established.
For this reason, the Buddha-dharma will quickly perish.
First, one must not obstruct others from leaving the household life. Second:
First, there is a general explanation of the five corruptions (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*);
second, from the section on the bhikṣus onwards, there is a specific explanation of seven matters.

As for what are called the five corruptions: first, the corruption of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*); second, the corruption of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*); third, the corruption of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*); fourth, the corruption of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*); and fifth, the corruption of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).

Second, following the section on bhikṣus, there is a separate clarification of seven matters: first, not permitting [certain persons] to leave the household life; second, not permitting the making of images and so forth; third, establishing an official head; fourth, maintaining registers to record the monks; fifth, not permitting a bhikṣu standing on the ground while a layperson sits on a high seat; sixth, not permitting soldiers or slaves to become bhikṣus; and seventh, not permitting the practice of accepting private invitations.
"The seven false dharmas arise and the seven true dharmas perish.

Great King! This destruction and confusion of my Way is your own doing; relying on your own power, you have oppressed my fourfold assembly of disciples. The common people suffer from disease and hardship without exception; this is the cause and condition for the ruin of the nation. To speak of the transgressions of the five turbidities would not be exhausted even in an entire kalpa."
"Great King, you have brought disorder to my Way by appointing secular officials to govern the Sangha.

To speak of relying on one's own power and authority to control the fourfold assembly of disciples means that, beyond the five categories and seven groups of precepts, you have further employed secular laws to punish bhikṣus and others. Because the Dharma-protecting benevolent deities are incensed, they have caused disease and the destruction of the nation, leading to the increase of the five turbidities."
“Great King!

In the final age of the Dharma, there will be bhikṣus among the fourfold assembly of disciples, and kings and ministers will each engage in unrighteous conduct. They will arbitrarily commit great unrighteous acts against the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha, committing various transgressions. Unlawfully and contrary to the Vinaya, they will bind the bhikṣus as if they were prisoners. At such a time, the extinction of the Dharma will be near.”
"O Great King, according to the Dharma, during the final age, one must not bind a bhikṣu like a prisoner in a jail.
Within the ultimate bounds of the Vinaya Dharma, there is only the act of banishing the monastic community;
now that you practice worldly laws, you should know that the extinction of the Dharma will not be long in coming."
“Great King!

After my parinirvāṇa, in future ages, among the fourfold assembly of disciples, it will be the minor kings, crown princes, and sons of kings who shall be those entrusted with upholding and protecting the Triple Gem, yet they will instead further destroy and dismantle the Triple Gem. They are like worms within a lion’s body that consume the lion itself; they are not outsiders.”
They will greatly destroy my Buddha-dharma and incur great transgressions.
The true teaching will decline and become thin, and the people will lack correct conduct.
Gradually becoming more evil, their lifespans will diminish day by day until they reach one hundred years.

When people destroy the Buddha’s teachings, there will no longer be filial sons; the six relations will live in discord, and the celestial deities will offer no protection. Epidemics and malevolent spirits will come daily to inflict harm.

Calamities and portents will follow one after another, with disasters spreading in all directions. Those who die will enter the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals; if they emerge as humans again, they will become soldiers or slaves.
"Karmic retribution is like an echo or a shadow; it is like a person writing at night, where the characters remain even after the fire is extinguished.
The karmic retributions of the three realms are likewise.

"Great King, after my parinirvāṇa, I shall issue a fourth admonition to the fourfold assembly, including kings and others, who are all those entrusted with upholding the Buddha-dharma. Yet they will instead destroy it themselves, causing various calamities to arise simultaneously throughout their lands; all this is brought about by their destruction of the Dharma."
The text consists of two parts:
first, an explanation of preaching the sutras in a manner contrary to the Dharma;
second, from "the True Dharma declines and thins" onwards, an explanation of its resulting losses.
First, the explanation of what is not the Dharma in the discourse on the sūtras has three parts:
first, the explanation by way of the Dharma;
second, "like a lion" and so forth; [and third, the conclusion].
This is the analogy;
thirdly, "the widespread destruction of my Buddha-dharma" below is the application of the parable.
Second, regarding the loss within, it refers to the decline and thinning of the True Dharma, whereby one encounters various kinds of suffering.
"Great King!

In future ages, all kings, crown princes, and sons of kings, as well as the fourfold assembly of disciples, will arbitrarily impose written precepts upon the disciples of the Buddha, modeled after the laws for laypeople or the laws for soldiers and slaves."
If my disciples—whether bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs—are registered in official records and compelled to serve the government, they are no longer my disciples at all; this is the law of military slaves.

To appoint a presiding official to oversee the Sangha and manage the monastic registers, with senior and junior Sangha-presidents binding one another in mutual restraint, is like the law of prisoners in a jail or the law of military slaves.
"At that time, the Buddha-dharma will not endure for long.

[The Buddha said: "Great King, in a future age, when the fifth admonition is issued to kings, crown princes, and the fourfold assembly, if they establish registers and regulations like those for military slaves, and appoint officials to govern the people according to secular laws, you should know that the extinction of the Buddha-dharma will likewise not be long delayed."
"Great King!

In future ages, various minor kings and their fourfold disciples will themselves commit these offenses, which become the causes and conditions for the destruction of their kingdoms; they shall receive the retribution for this in their own persons, and it shall not be the fault of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha."
"Great King, in future ages there will be various small kingdoms and lowly states; this is the sixth admonition for the fourfold assembly of those small kingdoms.
It clarifies that practicing what is not the Dharma incurs transgression, and it is enjoined that you must refrain from doing so."
"Committing offenses oneself and destroying the land, one receives the retribution for these deeds personally; it does not concern the Triple Gem.
'Great King!

In future ages, this sutra shall circulate as the vessel of the Buddhas of the seven periods and the path constantly traversed by the Buddhas of the ten directions. Yet, wicked bhikṣus who greedily seek fame and profit will themselves proclaim before kings, crown princes, and sons of kings the causes and conditions for the destruction of the Buddha-dharma and the destruction of the kingdom. If the king does not discern the truth but believes and listens to these words, arbitrarily establishing laws and regulations that do not rely on the Buddha's precepts, this constitutes the cause and condition for the destruction of the Buddha and the destruction of the kingdom.'"
"At that time, the True Dharma will not long remain before it perishes.

After the Great King has caused this sutra to circulate in future ages, he will issue a seventh admonition to the bhikṣus who do not rely on the seven teachings of the Buddha, but instead rely upon the Buddha-dharma to seek worldly fame and profit, going before kings to speak of their own reasons for destroying the Buddha-dharma.
The text has three distinct sections:
first, it clarifies how bhikṣus and others misinterpret the Buddha-dharma;
second, from "That king could not distinguish" onwards, it clarifies that the king did not understand the Three Jewels.
Third, at that time, the True Dharma will perish.

At that moment, when the sixteen great kings hear the Buddha’s exposition of future events within the Seven Admonitions, they weep and wail so bitterly that their voices shake the trichiliocosm; the sun, moon, five planets, and twenty-eight lunar mansions lose their radiance and cease to appear.

At that time, the various kings each received and upheld the Buddha’s words with a sincere heart; they would not restrict the fourfold assembly of disciples from leaving home to practice the Way, but would act in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching.
At that time, the great assembly—the eighteen Brahma kings and the various devaputras of the six heavens of desire—all exclaimed in lamentation:
"At such a time as this, the world is empty and void; it is an age without a Buddha."

At that time, following the section on the sixteen kingdoms, this is the third major division of the text. It concerns how the various kings, upon hearing that the Buddha’s seven admonitions did not restrict the fourfold assembly, divided the passage into two parts:
first, the sixteen kings lament with grief and alarm, grieving for their own past transgressions, and then follow the teaching by not restricting the fourfold assembly.

The twenty-eighth [chapter] records the lamentations of Brahmā and others, who exclaimed: "At such a time as this, the world is empty; this is an age without a Buddha. They grieved that the True Dharma had been extinguished, and thus it is called an "age without a Buddha."

At that time, among the immeasurable great assembly—consisting of ten billion bodhisattvas such as Maitreya and Siṃhacandra; ten billion Śāriputras and Subhūtis; five hundred billion Brahmās of the eighteen heavens and the various devas of the six heavens of the desire realm; and the asura kings of the three realms and the six paths of existence—hearing the Buddha’s teaching on the causes and conditions for protecting the fruit of buddhahood and the causes and conditions for protecting the land, they rejoiced immeasurably. They prostrated before the Buddha and received and upheld the Prajñāpāramitā.

From the passage "At that time, the immeasurable great assembly... onwards constitutes the fourth major section within this chapter: the assembly hears the Dharma and joyfully practices it in accordance with it.

This section consists of three parts: first, the listing of ten billion bodhisattvas; second, the listing of ten billion Śāriputras and others; and third, the five hundred billion devas of the desire and form realms, the six classes of beings, the asura kings, and so forth—all of whom practice in accordance with the teaching.
